newsitem.title: INDIA: India should aim for futures market in gold.
newsitem.headline: India should aim for futures market in gold.

text.p: A futures market in gold in India is essential for orderly growth of the sector as the country liberalises its trade in the metal, government officials and traders said on Saturday.

"In my view the development of a futures market in gold is the essential prerequisite to the orderly development of a domestic gold market in the liberalised environment," K. Govindan, deputy managing director of the State Bank of India told a gold seminar.

Govindan said the liberalisation process in regard to purchase, sale and ownership of gold that began in 1991 would be carried forward in the coming years and a sea change in the gold market in India was expected.
"What we need is a full-fleged metal bourse," said Bhargava Vaidya, a bullion merchant.
A government committee on Capital Account Convertibility, headed by S. S. Tarapore, earlier this year said that there was a strong case for liberalising the overall policy regime on gold.

The committee had recommended that banks and institutions should be allowed to operate freely in both the domestic and global markets in gold, permitted to sell the metal to all Indian residents and offer gold denominated deposits and loans.
It also suggested that household gold should be mobilised and working capital gold loans should be provided to jewellery manufacturers and traders.
India has more than 9,500 tonnes of gold worth $115 billion mostly in private hands, more than eight percent of all the gold recovered by mankind in history.

India consumed 508 tonnes of gold in 1996 out of which 397 tonnes were from imports and 111 tonnes were domestically recycled. Nearly 25 percent of the domestic requirement comes in through smuggling.

The government's 1997-2002 export and import policy had also initiated steps towards gold banking in India by authorising the Reserve Bank of India to allot licences to qualified agencies for importing gold.

Currently only the State Bank of India and MMTC Ltd are allowed to import gold. Exporter of certain products are also eligible to be issued special import licences as incentives to enable them to import products like gold.
Govindan said government would have to take steps from now on if it planned to open up the gold sector by implementing the Tarapore committee recommendations.
He said a government committee on commodity hedging should study the hedging requirements of the gold industry.

Govindan said the feasibility of a commodity derivatives section for futures trading in the National Stock Exchange, should be examined and an over the counter (OTC) market comprising designated gold importing agencies, jewellers and goldsmiths should be developed.

He said government should also put in place standards, in line with global requirements, for measuring purity and weight of gold. It should also create the necessary infrastructure for assaying and hallmarking of gold and gold jewellery.
D.S. Solanki, a senior official of the Central Board of Excise and Customs, said significant demand for gold in India could continue to come from the domestic sector.
He said the future perspective of the policy should be to ensure that whatever gold came into the country was accounted for and came through the legal route.
